title: Job 22:1–11
context: Eliphaz the Temanite answers Job, after the narrator’s brief heading in 22:1. This is his third speech, and he now moves from general argument to specific charges: Job’s wickedness is great, he has taken pledges for nothing, stripped the naked, withheld water and bread, favored the mighty, and sent widows away empty. Those accusations are Eliphaz’s, not the narrator’s verdict. They stand in tension with the book’s opening portrait of Job as blameless and upright in 1:1, with the LORD’s own words in 1:8 and 2:3, and later with Job’s own account of his care for the poor, the widow, and the fatherless in 29:12–17 and in the oaths of chapter 31. The notes name those texts by reference and do not force them into one story; they also do not treat Eliphaz’s speech as the book’s doctrine. In 42:7 the LORD will tell Eliphaz that he and his two friends “have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.” That later word is allowed to do its own work and is not imported into every line here. Both traditions read the unit as a friend’s accusation, to be weighed against the narrator and against Job’s later self-description, without a party contrast over the charges themselves.

verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator says, “Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,” and the speech that follows is Eliphaz’s. The heading only names the speaker and does not endorse what he will say. Eliphaz has already spoken in chapters 4–5 and 15; this is his third turn.

Arminian readers take the heading as a real change of speaker, a friend’s reply, not the book’s own verdict on Job.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the line in the narrator’s mouth, a formula that introduces Eliphaz, not a guarantee that the coming charges are true.

Both traditions wait on the speech itself, and they do not treat this heading as doctrine.

verses.text: “Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphaz begins, “Can a man be profitable to God? Surely he who is wise is profitable to himself.” The question sets up a claim that God does not gain from human wisdom or righteousness. The thought will be used to deny that Job is suffering for his piety, and so to push the cause back onto Job’s sin. The speaker is Eliphaz.

Arminian readers hear a half-truth used as an argument: God is not in Job’s debt, but that fact does not by itself prove Job guilty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also let Eliphaz speak. God needs no profit from a creature; the step from that to Job’s supposed wickedness is Eliphaz’s inference, not yet shown.

Both traditions distinguish what is said about God’s self-sufficiency from the use Eliphaz will make of it against Job.

verses.text: Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that you are righteous? Or does it benefit him that you make your ways perfect?
verses.arminianNotes:
He asks, “Is it any pleasure to the Almighty that you are righteous? Or does it benefit him that you make your ways perfect?” The Almighty is not pictured as gaining from Job’s righteousness. Eliphaz uses that to undercut any thought that God is treating Job unfairly. The questions are his, and they already assume that Job’s claim to uprightness cannot explain the suffering.

Arminian readers grant that God is not benefited as if he lacked something, and they still refuse to let that cancel the narrator’s word that Job is upright.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also deny that God is in need of Job’s perfection, while keeping Eliphaz’s conclusion about Job’s case unendorsed.

Both traditions can share the denial that God profits from human righteousness, without accepting Eliphaz’s coming charges as the book’s verdict.

verses.text: Is it for your piety that he reproves you, that he enters with you into judgment?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Is it for your piety that he reproves you, that he enters with you into judgment?” Eliphaz treats Job’s suffering as God’s reproof and judgment, and he denies that piety is the reason for it. In his logic, if God is not judging Job for being pious, Job must be judged for sin. The prologue has already said that Job was ruined “without cause” as to guilt (2:3); that earlier word is not answered here, and it is not Eliphaz’s.

Arminian readers take the question as Eliphaz’s frame for the trial, a frame the opening of the book has already placed in doubt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the reproof-and-judgment reading as Eliphaz’s, set beside the LORD’s earlier word that Job was ruined without cause, without forcing the two speeches into one account.

Both traditions refuse to treat this question as the narrator’s explanation of Job’s losses.

verses.text: Isn’t your wickedness great? Neither is there any end to your iniquities.
verses.arminianNotes:
The charge is now direct: “Isn’t your wickedness great? Neither is there any end to your iniquities.” Eliphaz invents a specific moral case against Job, not merely a general theory that sufferers must be sinners. The accusation is his. It stands against 1:1, 1:8, and 2:3, where Job is called blameless and upright, and against Job’s later account in 29:12–17 and chapter 31. Those texts should be named, not blended into a harmony that erases the conflict.

Arminian readers hear a grave charge that the book has not supported, a friend’s inference presented as fact.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the sentence in Eliphaz’s mouth. Great wickedness and endless iniquities are what he asserts; they are not the narrator’s verdict, and they are not the LORD’s words in the prologue.

Both traditions set the charge beside those other texts by reference, without a party contrast over Eliphaz’s error.

verses.text: For you have taken pledges from your brother for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphaz specifies, “For you have taken pledges from your brother for nothing, and stripped the naked of their clothing.” Job is accused of cruel dealing in pledges and of leaving people unclothed. Chapter 31 will later have Job deny that he has seen the needy without covering, or withheld clothing; 29:12–17 will describe him as delivering the poor. Those later lines are Job’s, as this is Eliphaz’s; they should be set side by side, not merged.

Arminian readers take the pledge-and-clothing charge as a concrete accusation without evidence given in this speech, a portrait that conflicts with the book’s opening estimate of Job.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also report the charge as Eliphaz’s invention of a crime, to be read against Job’s later oaths and against 1:1, 1:8, and 2:3, without harmonizing the accounts into one.

Both traditions keep the speaker clear and refuse to treat the accusation as established fact.

verses.text: You haven’t given water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You haven’t given water to the weary to drink, and you have withheld bread from the hungry.” The charge is hard-heartedness toward the weary and the hungry. Job will later say that the fatherless ate of his morsel and that he did not eat alone (31:16–17), and that he delivered the poor who cried (29:12). Again the two pictures are to be named, not forced into one.

Arminian readers hear Eliphaz attributing to Job the very neglect Job will deny, a specific sin the prologue has not hinted at.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set this withholding of water and bread beside Job’s later self-description and beside the narrator’s opening verdict, without declaring a harmony.

Both traditions leave the contradiction visible, and they invent no contrast between the traditions over it.

verses.text: But as for the mighty man, he had the earth. The honorable man, he lived in it.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But as for the mighty man, he had the earth. The honorable man, he lived in it.” The force of the lines is debated: Eliphaz may be saying that Job sided with the powerful, or that the land was left to the mighty while the weak were pushed aside. The notes do not settle a nuance the sentence leaves tight. On any reading, the charge belongs with 22:6–9 as an account of injustice, and it remains Eliphaz’s account.

Arminian readers take the verse as part of the same accusation, a claim that power, not mercy, shaped the land under Job.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the mighty and the honorable in Eliphaz’s argument, a picture of social wrong, not a proven history, and not the book’s own summary of Job’s life.

Both traditions hedge the exact point of the couplet and refuse to build more on it than the speech itself makes clear.

verses.text: You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You have sent widows away empty, and the arms of the fatherless have been broken.” The last of this set of charges names widows and the fatherless, the very people Job will later say he helped: the widow’s heart sang for joy, and he was a father to the needy (29:13, 29:16); he will swear he has not lifted his hand against the fatherless (31:21–22). Eliphaz’s picture and Job’s picture cannot be made the same without erasing one of them. The notes name both and leave the conflict standing. The narrator’s 1:1 and the LORD’s 1:8 and 2:3 already sit against Eliphaz’s charge as well.

Arminian readers hear a charge of cruelty to widows and orphans that the rest of the book does not corroborate, and that Job will formally deny.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the widows and the fatherless as Eliphaz names them, an accusation to be read beside 29:12–17, chapter 31, and the prologue, without forcing a single blended report.

Both traditions keep the two accounts side by side and refuse to treat Eliphaz’s charge as established fact.

verses.text: Therefore snares are around you. Sudden fear troubles you,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Therefore snares are around you. Sudden fear troubles you,” Eliphaz treats Job’s present terror and the snares around him as the consequence of the sins just listed. The “therefore” is his logic: great wickedness explains sudden fear. The prologue has given another account of the losses. The notes do not repeat that account at length; they only refuse to let Eliphaz’s “therefore” become the book’s.

Arminian readers take the snares and the fear as real in Job’s experience, and they reject Eliphaz’s causal claim as unproved.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also distinguish Job’s fear, which is described, from Eliphaz’s explanation, which is not the narrator’s.

Both traditions keep the verse as a friend’s inference, not as a finished theodicy.

verses.text: or darkness, so that you can not see, and floods of waters cover you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliphaz adds, “or darkness, so that you can not see, and floods of waters cover you.” Darkness and flood complete the picture of judgment he thinks Job has earned. The language is conventional for disaster; it is still tied, in his speech, to the charges of 22:5–9.

Arminian readers hear the darkness and the waters as Eliphaz’s description of Job’s state, offered as proof of guilt, which the book has not granted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the darkness and the floods in Eliphaz’s mouth, a rhetorical close to the first movement of the speech, not the book’s own interpretation of the ash heap.

Both traditions end the unit with the accusation still unproven, and with no party contrast over the images.
